routes.description: Establish that belief in Jesus' resurrection is reasonable through a cumulative historical inference from Jesus' death, the reported empty tomb and appearances, witness transformations, early proclamation, and comparison with rival explanations.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if its principal historical claims are adequately supported, bodily resurrection explains their conjunction better than the live alternatives, and the evidential standard permits supernatural causation to be inferred without first assuming it.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative historical and explanatory case to the conclusion that belief in Jesus' bodily resurrection is epistemically reasonable.

centralBridges.description: Establish the material historical data concerning death, burial or the empty tomb, reported appearances, conversions, and early resurrection proclamation.
Show that bodily resurrection has greater explanatory scope and power than conspiracy, hallucination, legend, error, or combinations of natural alternatives.
Show that the event's religious context and the failure of competing explanations warrant identifying the resurrection as divine action.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Support the historical sources through their asserted earliness, multiplicity, local detail, cultural fit, archaeology, and relevant scholarly agreement.
Defend ordinary cumulative historical reasoning against standards alleged to exclude extraordinary conclusions categorically or generate an evidential regress.

routes.description: Establish that belief in Jesus' resurrection is unreasonable because transmitted reports, disputed historical premises, and background compatibility do not provide sufficient warrant for either the event or its supernatural cause.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the available sources do not adequately establish the material premises, ordinary explanations or unresolved uncertainty remain live, or the evidence fails to meet the burden appropriate to an extraordinary supernatural conclusion.

motionBridge.description: Connect the insufficiency and underdetermination of the available evidence to withholding belief in bodily resurrection as the reasonable position.

centralBridges.description: Show that late, dependent, disputed, or second- and third-hand reports cannot securely establish the proposed resurrection facts.
Show that sincerity, movement growth, accurate background details, and reported experiences remain compatible with legend, error, transmission, or unknown causes.
Require evidence not only that an unusual event occurred but also that resurrection was possible and that supernatural or divine causation produced it.
Apply an evidential burden proportionate to the extraordinariness and low background plausibility of bodily resurrection.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish reports, sincere beliefs, and incidental historical accuracy from independent support for the resurrection proposition itself.
Defend suspension of judgment without requiring a complete rival reconstruction or a claim that resurrection is impossible.

sections.title: Historical facts and source reliability
sections.rationale: The cumulative inference depends on whether death, burial, the empty tomb, appearances, conversions, and early proclamation are established by sufficiently early, independent, consistent, and reliable sources.

sections.title: Testimony, sincerity, and corroboration
sections.rationale: The parties dispute what reported experiences, costly commitment, local knowledge, archaeology, and accurate background details can establish about the central resurrection claims.

sections.title: Resurrection and rival explanations
sections.rationale: The motion turns substantially on whether resurrection explains the proposed historical data better than legend, deception, hallucination, error, transmission, combined alternatives, or unresolved uncertainty.

sections.title: Event evidence and supernatural causation
sections.rationale: Evidence for an unusual return to life and evidence that God caused a bodily resurrection are distinct inferential questions whose connection is necessary to the motion.

sections.title: Extraordinary claims and evidential burden
sections.rationale: The appropriate relationship among prior plausibility, extraordinary claims, proportional evidence, and historical inference determines what support reasonable belief requires.

sections.title: Reasonable belief and suspension of judgment
sections.rationale: The ultimate burden requires deciding whether the cumulative case warrants belief or whether remaining evidential uncertainty makes suspension of judgment the justified motion-level conclusion.

chunk-001:c001.proposition: Belief in Jesus' resurrection can be reasonable when likely historical facts are established and competing explanations of those facts are compared cumulatively.

chunk-001:c002.proposition: Jesus' death by Roman crucifixion under Pontius Pilate is a securely supported historical foundation for assessing the resurrection claim.

chunk-001:c003.proposition: Jesus was probably buried in a private tomb later found empty, supported by considerations including multiple attestation, women witnesses, Joseph of Arimathea, and archaeology.

chunk-001:c004.proposition: Individual and group experiences understood as appearances of the risen Jesus form historical data that ordinary hallucination does not adequately explain.

chunk-001:c005.proposition: The disciples' transformed lives and willingness to endure persecution support the inference that they sincerely believed they had encountered the risen Jesus.

chunk-001:c007.proposition: Jesus' religious, miraculous, and prophetic context indicates that, if he rose, the event is best understood as an act of God.

chunk-001:c010.proposition: Resurrection explains the cumulative historical data better than conspiracy, hallucination, legend, or combinations of those natural rival explanations.

chunk-003:chunk-003-candidate-01.proposition: Detailed knowledge of Palestinian institutions, geography, and customs cumulatively corroborates the historical reliability of the Gospel reporting.

chunk-003:chunk-003-candidate-03.proposition: A case combining reasonably established nonmiraculous historical facts with resurrection as their best explanation need not prove its conclusion before its supporting evidence is considered.

chunk-003:chunk-003-candidate-06.proposition: Paul's language and relevant Jewish historical concepts indicate that the earliest resurrection claim concerned Jesus' bodily resurrection rather than a merely spectral experience.

chunk-004:c004-03.proposition: A categorical demand for extraordinary evidence risks an evidential regress because each extraordinary item of support can itself be treated as another claim requiring further support.

chunk-005:chunk005-candidate-10.proposition: First-century evidence supports resurrection belief, while accumulated historical research enables present investigators to assess the events surrounding Jesus' death and claimed resurrection thoughtfully.

chunk-002:c002-01.proposition: Sincere testimony can support that an extraordinary experience was reported without sufficiently establishing that its supernatural interpretation is true.

chunk-002:c002-03.proposition: Resurrection cannot serve as the best explanation unless the possibility of supernatural interaction is supported rather than exempted from ordinary evidential standards.

chunk-002:c002-04.proposition: Known sources of false reports, including deception, legend, error, and exaggeration, remain better-grounded candidates than an unsupported resurrection mechanism.

chunk-002:c002-06.proposition: Noncontemporary and source-dependent accounts with unresolved inconsistencies do not securely convert the proposed minimal-facts list into established historical facts.

chunk-002:c002-07.proposition: Rejecting selected natural alternatives does not establish resurrection when information is incomplete and unknown possibilities remain, so insufficient evidence warrants uncertainty.

chunk-003:chunk-003-candidate-04.proposition: Concluding that resurrection has not met its burden is compatible with leaving its occurrence possible and does not assume that supernatural events cannot occur.

chunk-003:chunk-003-candidate-05.proposition: The reported crucifixion lacks contemporary verification, while the absence of independent reports for associated conspicuous events weakens confidence in the narrative source.

chunk-003:chunk-003-candidate-07.proposition: Paul's third-party reports of appearances do not establish that the named witnesses personally attested as claimed or that a resurrection actually occurred.

chunk-004:c004-01.proposition: Even direct confirmation that Jesus returned to life would not by itself identify either a supernatural mechanism or divine agency as the cause.

chunk-004:c004-02.proposition: Bodily resurrection is an extraordinary claim whose lack of physical, contemporary, and possibility-establishing evidence leaves the available support insufficient.

chunk-004:c004-05.proposition: The quantity and quality of evidence required for warranted belief should scale with a claim's extraordinariness and overcome well-supported conflicting background beliefs.

chunk-005:chunk005-candidate-04.proposition: Unresolved textual problems and the absence of evidence beyond resurrection reports make suspension of judgment more reasonable than accepting resurrection as an explanation.
